opening.headline: We explore a method to address the problem of context waste caused by repeatedly explaining the same procedure in prompts by replacing it with a procedure handbook that is read only when necessary—referred to as a skill.
body: If, every time requesting a procedure to extract tables from PDFs and fill out forms, we append forty lines of instructions to the prompt, what would happen? The same guidelines would be repeatedly included in the context for each conversation, leading to slightly different versions across team members. Conversely, if we embed all instructions into the system prompt, inactive procedures would still consume context space.

Agent Skills bundles instructions, execution code, and reference materials into a single directory and loads them only when needed. In this course, we examine the structure of skills, the principle of progressive disclosure in loading, principles for using effective skills, and differentiate skills from tools.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can describe the structure of Agent Skills and their progressive disclosure (step-by-step loading).
Can distinguish the difference between skills and tools, and can judge what is appropriate given a particular situation.

screens.title: Describes the same procedure each time as a prompt.
screens.lead: Read about the two wastes that arise when procedures are handled solely through prompts. The diagram compares the context being consumed.

visual.alt: Comparison between a 40-line instruction being repeatedly inserted into the context of each conversation, and a scenario where only the name and description are displayed, with the full text appearing only when needed.

paragraphs: A team frequently extracts tables from PDFs and fills out forms. Every time this procedure is requested, they append 40 lines to the prompt. This then leads to two problems.

First, the same instructions are repeatedly added to the context for each conversation, reducing the space available for other information. As team members start using slightly different versions of these instructions, the process may diverge. Second, if all instructions are included in the system prompt to avoid this, unnecessary procedures are always added to the context for every request.

If there exists a procedure that is loaded only when needed, this waste disappears. Normally, one simply knows that such a procedure exists, and only when a relevant request comes in is it expanded and accessed. Agent Skills take exactly this form. Once a skill is created, it is automatically reused across multiple conversations.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: A prompt is a one-time instruction for a conversation. What costs will continue if we only treat repetitive procedures as one-time instructions? Answer it again when the lesson is over.

screens.outro: First, let's recall whether you have any frequently used guidelines.

screens.title: Preview: Reusable instructions
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Where in the text is the same phrase being repeated in each conversation?
items.answer: Procedural elements such as report templates, code review criteria, and file processing methods are typical examples. These guidelines serve as candidates for skills. It is more efficient to store them in one place and refer to them when needed rather than copying and pasting frequently.

items.prompt: Most of the requests in this guideline are unnecessary; what specific portions are required only for certain requests?
items.answer: For example, end-of-month closing exception procedures or special formatting rules. Such aspects should never be context-bound. Skills separate these contents into a separate file and read them only when the corresponding request is made.

items.prompt: Are there any scripts or reference materials that need to be executed together with these instructions?
items.answer: This includes scripts, data schemas, and templates. Skills may contain not only instructions but also execution code and reference materials within the same directory. It means managing procedures and their associated materials as a single unit.

screens.outro: Let's substitute the considered procedure into the skill's structure.

screens.title: Agent Skills Structure
screens.lead: When you select the image number marker, you can view each section of the skill directory in detail. Please select them sequentially from number 1.

visual.alt: Diagram of the tree structure containing the pdf-processing skills directory with SKILL.md, FORMS.md, REFERENCE.md, and a scripts folder.
labels: description: Extracts text and tables from PDFs and fills out forms. Used when performing PDF operations.

markers.label: Skill Directory
markers.title: A skill is a folder.
markers.body: A skill is a directory containing instructions, executable code, and reference materials. It is structured similarly to an onboarding guide designed for new team members. Within an environment that allows access to the file system, the model can explore this directory as if it were a regular file. Pre-built skills (such as PowerPoint, Excel, Word, PDF) and custom skills created by users function in the same way.

markers.label: Preface
markers.title: SKILL.md Introduction: name and description
markers.body: SKILL.md is a required file and contains a YAML header with name and description fields. The name may only include lowercase letters, digits, and hyphens. The description must fully explain what the skill does and when it should be used, and must not exceed 1,024 characters. The model selects one of hundreds of skills based on seeing this sentence.

markers.label: Body
markers.title: SKILL.md Body: Procedural Knowledge
markers.body: Below the heading, the body contains procedural knowledge such as workflow, best practices, and guidance. Skills only become contextually active when they are invoked. To remain concise, the body competes with other information and conversation history, so it is kept brief as it grows longer.

markers.label: Reference document
markers.title: FORMS.md, REFERENCE.md: Separate documents
markers.body: Optional content such as formatting guidelines or detailed API references is separated into standalone documents. When SKILL.md references this document, the model only reads it when necessary. Files that are not read incur no context cost.

markers.label: script
markers.title: scripts/: code to be executed
markers.body: Scripts such as fill_form.py are executed by the model via bash. The actual code does not enter the context; only the execution results are provided, making them suitable for deterministic and reproducible tasks. To use a skill through an API, a container containing the execution tool for the skill's code is required.

screens.outro: Having verified the structure, we will now examine the principle of gradual disclosure, which is the mechanism by which context is preserved.

screens.title: Gradual disclosure: three-stage loading
screens.lead: The following table organizes the content of skills into three stages based on when they are loaded into context. Read it from top to bottom and verify how token costs differ at each stage.

data.caption: Skill content being uploaded in three stages to the context
rows: Only the name and description of each skill are uploaded to the system prompt.
When the request matches the description, the skill is activated.
The model reads SKILL.md in bash and the body is incorporated into the context.
Only when the file pointed to by SKILL.md is needed
Documents like FORMS.md load when read, while scripts only load their execution results.
data.notes: Even with many skills installed, under normal circumstances they only occupy context with their names and descriptions. For example, when a PDF request arrives, the system reads only the SKILL.md file for the PDF skill, and reads the FORMS.md file only if form filling is required. This step-by-step loading of only what is necessary is called progressive disclosure. Since the three-stage materials do not consume tokens until they are actually read, even large schemas or documents can be included without burden. As a file-system-based structure, instructions offer flexibility, code ensures reliability, and data provides accurate factual retrieval.

screens.outro: Now that you understand structure and loading, let's examine the principles of using effective skills.

screens.title: Skill Design Best Practices
screens.lead: When designing skills by selecting each tab, learn the principles you should follow.

tabs.label: Conciseness
tabs.body:
The context window is a public resource. Skills utilize the system prompt, conversation history, metadata from other skills, and actual user requests, distributing them across the context. Therefore, the model only generates content for what it does not already know, avoiding repetition of information it already possesses.

As shown in document examples, a lengthy explanation describing what a PDF is amounts to approximately 150 tokens, while a concise description including code about which library is used for text extraction is about 50 tokens. Since both serve the same purpose, the shorter version is preferable.

tabs.label: degree of freedom
tabs.body:
The specificity of instructions is determined by how easily a task can break. Code reviews that vary by context are left with high flexibility through textual guidelines. If preferred patterns exist, intermediate flexibility is provided via parameterized scripts. Tasks that are prone to breaking—such as database migrations—are fixed with precise commands to reduce flexibility.

The document includes an analogy that in a narrow bridge with steep sides, precise guidance is required, whereas in a risk-free open field, only general direction is needed.

tabs.label: structure
tabs.body: SKILL.md keeps the main content under 500 lines and splits detailed sections into separate files, referenced directly within SKILL.md with only one level of depth. By dividing reference files by domain—such as finance, sales, or product—queries about sales metrics will only read the sales-specific file, reducing token usage. Reference files exceeding 100 lines must include a table of contents at the top.

tabs.label: Name and Description
tabs.body: The name should follow a similar pattern to `processing-pdfs`, using only lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens. The description should include both what the item does and when it is used. A good example is "Extracts text and tables from PDFs and fills out forms. Use this when working with PDFs." Avoid vague phrases such as `Helps with documents` or `Processes data`. The model would otherwise have to choose among hundreds or even thousands of skills based solely on such a sentence.

tabs.label: Test
tabs.body:
Skills are tested across all models since they are added to the model. We check whether Haiku has sufficient guidance, whether Sonnet has clear and efficient guidance, and whether Opus avoids excessive explanation. Opus may require more detailed content than Haiku. 

Additionally, since skills are read and executed by the model, only trusted skills are used, and all bundled files (SKILL.md, scripts, images) are reviewed before use.

screens.outro: Having examined the principles and fundamentals, let us now illustrate the process of turning a practical, repeated procedure into a skill.

screens.title: Case Explanation: Creating a procedure as a skill reduces context overhead.
screens.lead: The instructor explains the process of turning the weekly report writing procedure into a skill. Select the right arrow to proceed step by step.

visual.alt: Weekly report showing the directory structure of skills and files loaded by request type.
labels: SKILL.md only the heading is uploaded
Load SKILL.md and MONTH_END.md, execute chart script

steps.title: Verify the example
steps.body: A team includes four explanations in their prompt every time they write a weekly report: format rules, glossary of terms, end-of-month reconciliation exception procedures, and a script for generating charts. Since this explanation is appended with every request, context is wasted and team members end up with different versions.

steps.title: Step 1: Disassemble
steps.body: The content is always necessary, occasionally necessary, or executable. Report generation flow is always necessary. Monthly closing and terminology dictionary are occasionally necessary. Chart scripts are executable via code.

steps.title: Step 2: Package it
steps.body:
The writing flow is placed in the SKILL.md document. Month-end reconciliation is handled in MONTH_END.md, and terminology is kept in a separate GLOSSARY.md document, referenced from SKILL.md. Charts are stored in the scripts/ folder. The header is written as follows:

```yaml
---
name: writing-weekly-reports
description: Creates weekly team reports in a standardized format and generates charts. Used when preparing weekly or month-end reconciliation reports.
---
```

The name follows the direct noun form, and the description includes both the purpose and when it is used.

steps.title: Step 3: Compare the loadings
steps.body: In regular conversations, the context contains only the name and description of this skill. It is approximately 100 tokens in length. When a weekly report request is received, the model reads the content of SKILL.md. Only when a monthly report request is received does the model read MONTH_END.md. Chart scripts are executed, and only the results are added to the context. Using a vocabulary dictionary that is not actively utilized incurs no cost.

steps.title: Step 4: Summarize the results
steps.body: General conversation context is reduced. Instructions, when updated in one place, are reflected everywhere, so version splits across team members do not occur. Special procedures like end-of-month processes only incur costs when needed. Both wastes associated with the first screen are eliminated.

screens.outro: Since the principle has been verified, let's distinguish what makes a skill different from a tool.

screens.title: What is the difference between skill and tool?
screens.lead: Alternate between the two states and compare the nature of the tools and skills. Finally, you can verify the design that combines both.

states.label: tools
states.body:
A tool is an executable function called by a model. It interacts with external systems or performs computations. The definition of a tool (name, description, parameters) is instantiated into the model's context on each request. When the model observes the definition and requests a call, the application executes the function and returns the result.

For example, a function that creates a ticket in a ticketing system is a tool. Because it involves integration with an external system, it cannot be accomplished solely with the model's knowledge or instructions and must therefore be provided as a callable function.

states.label: skill
states.body:
A skill is a bundle of procedures and knowledge that a model accesses when needed. Names and descriptions are always present, while the body and materials are loaded only when required. Unlike prompts that disappear after each conversation, skills are reusable across conversations.

For example, report-writing rules constitute a skill. Because they involve recurring methods and knowledge, it is efficient to define them once and retrieve them when needed. By placing a script within a skill, it gains executable capabilities akin to a tool, and in this case, only the execution results are included in the context.

The distinction is simple: if an action involves accessing external systems, it's a tool; if it involves recurring methods and knowledge, it's a skill. Combining both is a common design pattern. For instance, you can have both a ticket-creation tool and a skill that specifies how to write a ticket based on certain criteria.

screens.outro: Since we've completed the categorization, I'll summarize the key points in one slide.

screens.title: Summarize a skill into one entry
screens.lead: We summarize and organize the previous content into three categories: structure, loading, and differentiation.

paragraphs: The skill is a directory containing SKILL.md, reference materials, and scripts. The name and description in the header serve as the basis for the model selecting a skill, so the description should include both what the skill does and when it should be used.

Loading occurs only when necessary, in the order of metadata, SKILL.md body, references, and scripts. Thanks to this progressive disclosure, even if many skills are installed, under normal circumstances each skill only occupies context with its name and description. Scripts only contribute execution results to the context, not the code itself.

When designing, exclude content that the model already knows, make instructions more specific as the workflow becomes more complex, and break down details into separate files. Also remember to distinguish skills as procedures and knowledge, and tools as callable functions.

Going back to the initial question, when repetitive procedures are handled solely through one-time prompts, the cost includes context waste from repeatedly loading the same instructions for each conversation, as well as management overhead from version divergence. Skills address this by packaging the procedures once. When a change is made in one place, it is reflected everywhere, and unused procedures do not consume context.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: A skill is a procedural guide to be read when needed. Only the name and description are always available, while the main content and materials are loaded only when necessary.

checks.intro: Just verify the loading order you recently learned on your own. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: When a skill processes a request, consider the order in which contexts are added.
items: At startup, only the name and description of each skill are uploaded to the system prompt.
If the request matches the description, the SKILL.md body is read.
Read the reference documentation pointed to by SKILL.md when needed
If a script is needed, execute it and only the result is entered into the context.
checks.explain: Metadata is uploaded only when SKILL.md is active, when reference materials are accessed, or when scripts are referenced. Files that are not read incur no token cost.

checks.intro: The issue is distinguishing skills from tools. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: There are functions for accessing an external ticket system to create tickets, as well as a bundle of report writing rules. What is the appropriate distinction?
options: Both are created as skills to be read when needed.
Ticket creation is a skill; the rules are made with tools.
Both are defined as tools, with definitions loaded every time.
Ticket creation is made with tools, and the writing rules are crafted with skills.
checks.explain: Execution functions for accessing external systems are tools, while recurring methods and knowledge are appropriate reading skills to be acquired when needed. A design that combines both is possible.

wrong.0: External system access is a callable feature, i.e., the responsibility of the tool.
wrong.1: The roles are reversed. Access functions are tools and rule bundles are skills.
wrong.2: Once even the writing rules are treated as a tool, the definition remains attached to each request and occupies the context when not in use.

glossary.def: This approach involves bundling guidelines, execution code, and reference materials into a single directory, where the model can read from and write to them as needed.
This is a required file for skills. It has name and description in the YAML header at the top, followed by procedural knowledge below.
Metadata, body, references, and code are loaded into context incrementally at required points.
A sentence that specifies what a skill does and when it should be used, serving as the basis for the model to select among multiple skills.
This indicates how specific the skill's instructions are. The lower the value, the more precise the command, especially for easily breakable tasks.

misconceptions.myth: The more skills you install, the larger the context they occupy.
misconceptions.fact: When starting up, only about 100 tokens of skill names and descriptions are loaded, so the overhead of installation is minimal. The main content and materials are loaded only when needed.

misconceptions.myth: It is safer to write out all content in great detail in SKILL.md.
misconceptions.fact: The body states that when a skill is activated, it takes context and competes with the conversation history. Write concisely, excluding any content the model knows, and break down details into separate files.

misconceptions.myth: A skill is merely another name for a prompt.
misconceptions.fact: A prompt is a one-time instruction for a conversation, while skills are reusable across conversations and loaded progressively. Execution code and reference materials can also be included.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: A skill is a procedural guide to be accessed when needed. Names and descriptions are always available, while the body content and materials are uploaded only when required.
The description includes both what is done and when it is used, while SKILL.md remains concise.
The degree of freedom of instructions is determined according to how easily the operation can break.
A tool is a function that is called, while a skill is a procedure that is executed; therefore, they are distinguished according to their purpose and used together.
